passage: I'm Pema, and I've shared a flat with Jyoti in Bengaluru for two years. Every second Thursday at six, she leaves for what she calls her "brain dentist". For a long time I assumed something was badly wrong. Once I asked, carefully, and she laughed. "Nothing's wrong. That's the point. I go so small things don't become big things." She had started after a hard breakup, she said, and kept going when life got better, the way you keep brushing after the toothache stops. I noticed she argued less with her mother on those Thursday nights, and she handled a bad appraisal in March without the week-long silence I'd seen before. She told me she had switched counsellors once, because the first one kept giving advice instead of listening. Last month, in my own rough patch, she didn't push. She just left her centre's number on the fridge. I called it on a Thursday.

qa.q: What does Jyoti call her counsellor?
qa.a: Her brain dentist.

qa.q: What might Jyoti have felt when Pema asked carefully about the Thursdays?
qa.a: Jyoti seemed relaxed and amused, laughing, not at all ashamed of going to therapy.

qa.q: What does Jyoti's approach show about choosing appropriate help?
qa.a: Treat counselling as regular maintenance, and switch counsellors if the fit is wrong, for example to one who listens rather than lectures.

qa.q: How has Pema's view of therapy changed?
qa.a: Pema first assumed something was badly wrong, but after seeing Jyoti handle hard moments calmly, Pema called the centre too.

grounding: A flatmate observes a young woman treating counselling as ordinary maintenance and choosing the right counsellor.

passage:
September. Rukmini had been snapping at everyone since her promotion. When Lalit suggested counselling, she laughed. "Therapy is for people with real problems." She tried to fix it with more gym.
October. Still sleeping badly, she went, half to prove Lalit wrong, to a free peer-support circle at the community centre. Eight people, one volunteer facilitator, no advice, just listening. A man her age described exactly the tight chest she felt every Sunday night. She didn't speak. But she came back the next week.
December. The facilitator mentioned that some things need more than a circle, and gave her the name of a counsellor with a sliding fee. Rukmini booked a first session, cancelled it, then booked again. By the end of the month she had been four times, and she still went to the circle on Tuesdays. She told Lalit, "It's like the gym, but for the part of me I kept ignoring."

qa.q: How many people were in the peer-support circle?
qa.a: Eight people.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when she booked, cancelled and rebooked the session?
qa.a: Rukmini felt hesitant and nervous about counselling, torn between old beliefs and needing help.

qa.q: How did the peer circle help Rukmini find the right level of help?
qa.a: It made her feelings seem normal, and its facilitator pointed her to a counsellor when more support was needed.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel hearing Rukmini's gym comparison?
qa.a: Lalit would likely feel relieved and quietly pleased that the suggestion she laughed at became something useful.

grounding: Over months, a young woman moves from dismissing therapy to peer support and then counselling as ordinary care.

passage: Harsha, you think I'm the calmest person in this office. Let your old colleague Maria tell you a secret. When I was twenty-five, my father died in the spring and I went back to work after four days, because that's what we did. I was fine, I told everyone. By autumn I was crying in the printer room and forgetting meetings. My friend Nalini said, "See someone." I said therapy was for weak people. She said, "Then call it maintenance, like servicing a scooter." I went, grumbling. The first counsellor was wrong for me: all questions about my childhood, nothing about now. I nearly quit. Nalini said, "Try another, the way you'd try another doctor." The second one helped. I went for two years, stopped, and went again when my son was born. So when you say you're "just stressed", Harsha, I'm only saying: servicing is not failure.

qa.q: How many days after her father's death did Maria go back to work?
qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: What was young Maria feeling by the autumn?
qa.a: Maria was overwhelmed and grieving, crying in the printer room and forgetting meetings.

qa.q: What choice in Maria's story made therapy work for her?
qa.a: Trying a second counsellor instead of quitting after a poor first fit, as she would with another doctor.

qa.q: How might Nalini have felt pushing Maria to see someone?
qa.a: Nalini was probably worried about her friend but patient, reframing therapy as maintenance to get past Maria's resistance.

grounding: A senior colleague tells a younger one how she came to see counselling as ordinary maintenance after grief.

passage: Gargi's father's hospital stay lasted only three days, but it changed the question. At dinner afterwards he said, "I want you to take over the business next year." The business was his construction firm in Faridabad. Gargi was an environmental lawyer, and she had spent two years fighting firms that dumped debris on the Yamuna floodplains, firms not so different from his. The hospital scare had given everyone a deadline: decide by Diwali. She felt split in two. The daughter owed him; the lawyer couldn't pretend. She talked it through with Jyoti, a senior at her chambers. "You don't have to choose between being a good daughter and a good lawyer," Jyoti said. "You have to decide what you'd do with the company." Gargi went back to her father with a proposal: she would join as a part-time director and start by cleaning up debris disposal. He frowned a long time. Then he said, "Start with the Sector 12 site."

qa.q: Where was her father's construction firm?
qa.a: In Faridabad.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when her father asked her to take over?
qa.a: Gargi felt torn in two, between duty to her father and her values as an environmental lawyer.

qa.q: How did Jyoti's reframe help Gargi reconcile her roles?
qa.a: It shifted the question from choosing one identity to deciding what she would do with the company, leading to a proposal that honoured both.

qa.q: How might Gargi's father have seen her proposal?
qa.a: He probably felt challenged by the implied criticism but relieved she would join, which is why he named a site to start with.

grounding: Under a deadline after a family health scare, a young lawyer finds a way to join her father's firm without abandoning her values.

passage: For three years Hemant lived two lives in Chennai. By day he was the dependable eldest son and junior accountant who sent money home to Madurai every month. Three evenings a week he acted with a small Tamil theatre group in Mylapore and told his parents he was working late. Keerthana, who directed the group, noticed he always slipped away before the curtain-call photos. "Why hide?" she asked. "Because Appa thinks theatre is for people who've given up." "Have you given up?" Hemant thought of the audit files he closed carefully every week, the money he had never once missed sending. "No." "Then maybe you're one person, not two." Before the next show he called his parents, told them, and sent them bus tickets. Appa came, arms folded. In the second act, when Hemant's character forgave his father on stage, Appa's arms slowly unfolded.

qa.q: Where did the theatre group perform?
qa.a: In Mylapore.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he slipped away before the curtain-call photos?
qa.a: Hemant was anxious and ashamed of being found out, fearing his father's judgement.

qa.q: What helped Hemant bring his two lives together?
qa.a: Seeing he hadn't given up his duties, then telling his parents and inviting them, so both roles could be seen as one person.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt watching the second act?
qa.a: Appa probably arrived sceptical, arms folded, but was moved by the scene and softened towards his son's theatre.

grounding: A young man in Chennai stops hiding his theatre life from his parents and integrates duty and passion into one identity.

passage:
"Veerji, I got the Canada offer." Amandeep sat on the tubewell ledge beside his brother.
Gurpreet kept his eyes on the wheat. "Bebe will cry. Bapu will go silent."
"I know."
"And the farm?"
"That's what I've been thinking about for a month. I don't want to be the son who leaves and sends dollars. I also don't want to be the one who stays and resents it."
"So?"
"Two years. I'll learn soil technology there, the kind we need here. I'll come back every harvest. And you and I set up drip irrigation with my savings, together."
Gurpreet was quiet. "You've thought about it."
"Every night."
"Bapu will say you're choosing money over family."
"Then help me tell him it's both. He listens to you."
Gurpreet finally looked at him. "You'll call Bebe every Sunday."
"Every Sunday."
"Then I'll talk to Bapu."

qa.q: What will Amandeep learn in Canada?
qa.a: Soil technology, the kind needed on the farm.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling about leaving, judging from the talk?
qa.a: Amandeep felt torn and anxious, not wanting to abandon the family or to stay and resent it.

qa.q: How did Amandeep try to reconcile duty and ambition?
qa.a: By planning two years abroad, learning skills useful for the farm, returning each harvest and investing in irrigation with his brother.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet come to see his brother's plan?
qa.a: Gurpreet first thinks of the family's hurt, but seeing how carefully Amandeep planned, he agrees to talk to Bapu.

grounding: Two brothers on a Punjab farm work out how one can go abroad while keeping faith with family duty.

passage:
"I made the wrong choice," Vikas said, pushing his plate away. "I left a safe job for the startup, and it shut down in five months."
Lalit, his old college roommate, raised an eyebrow. "Was it a bad decision, or a bad result?"
"Same thing."
"Not really. What did you know when you chose?"
Vikas thought. "The founders were good. They had funding for eighteen months. The role was what I wanted."
"And what couldn't you know?"
"That their main client would pull out."
"So with what you knew, was it reasonable?"
"…Yes. Probably."
"Then it was a decent bet that lost. What would you check next time?"
"How many clients they depend on. I never asked that."
"That's the lesson. Not 'never take risks'."
Vikas breathed out. "Feels less like I'm an idiot."
"You're not. You're unlucky and slightly wiser."

qa.q: How long did the startup last after Vikas joined?
qa.a: Five months.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when he said he made the wrong choice?
qa.a: Vikas felt regretful and foolish, blaming himself for the shutdown.

qa.q: What question will Vikas add next time, and why does it help?
qa.a: How many clients the company depends on; it tests the risk he missed without swearing off all risk.

qa.q: How does Lalit see Vikas's decision?
qa.a: Lalit sees it as a reasonable bet that lost, and wants Vikas to separate the quality of the choice from the outcome.

grounding: A friend helps a young man judge a failed career move by the information he had, not the outcome.

passage: Last spring I, Damini, had to decide whether to move to Pune with Anirban, who had got a job there, without a job of my own. My gut said yes; my fear said I'd end up dependent and bitter. I didn't have enough information, so I stopped trying to decide all at once. First I asked my manager whether I could work remotely for three months. She agreed to two. Then I set a test: apply to twenty Pune firms in those two months and see what came back. I wrote down a prediction, too: "Maybe one interview." I got five. That surprised me, and I updated. By week seven I had an offer, though it paid less than I'd hoped. I took it anyway. Pune has been good, mostly. The commute is terrible. But I know the choice was made carefully, and that part I could control.

qa.q: How many interviews did Damini get?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling before the move?
qa.a: Damini felt torn and afraid, with a hopeful gut but a fear of becoming dependent and bitter.

qa.q: How did Damini decide despite missing information?
qa.a: By buying time with remote work, running a test of twenty applications, writing down a prediction, and updating when the results came in.

qa.q: How might Anirban have felt during those two months?
qa.a: Anirban was probably hopeful but anxious, wanting Damini to come without feeling pushed, and relieved when the offer came.

grounding: A young adult looks back on deciding to move cities with incomplete information by testing, predicting and updating.

passage: Operations lead's note, cyclone week. On Tuesday evening, with the cyclone's path still uncertain, Shankar (shift planner) had to decide whether to send twelve trucks south to Chennai overnight or hold them in Nellore. The forecasts disagreed. He listed what he knew, what he didn't, and what each choice would cost if wrong. He held eight trucks and sent four carrying urgent medical supplies by the inland road, with drivers checking in every two hours. At 2 a.m. the forecast shifted, and he pulled two trucks into a safe depot. In the end the cyclone turned north, so holding the eight cost us a day of deliveries. Some managers called it over-cautious. I disagree. With the information he had, the choice was sound, and he changed course as new information arrived. I've asked Shankar to write up his method for the team. — Manoj Pillai

qa.q: How many trucks did Shankar hold in Nellore?
qa.a: Eight trucks.

qa.q: What might Shankar have been feeling with the forecasts disagreeing?
qa.a: Shankar was probably tense and uncertain, responsible for drivers and supplies with no clear answer.

qa.q: What made Shankar's process sound even though the outcome cost a day?
qa.a: He listed knowns, unknowns and the cost of being wrong, split the risk, kept drivers checking in, and updated when the forecast changed.

qa.q: How does Manoj Pillai see the managers who called it over-cautious?
qa.a: Manoj disagrees with them, judging the decision by the information Shankar had rather than by how the storm turned out.

grounding: A manager's note shows a young planner making a sound decision under uncertainty and accepting an unlucky outcome.

subtype: Managing Anger, Envy & Ego at Work
passage: I'm Vasudha. I sat across from Tejas the morning the promotion email came. The team lead post went to Kunal, who had joined a year after Tejas. I watched Tejas read the email, go very still, and close his laptop. He walked out for twenty minutes. When he came back he was red around the eyes, but he went straight to Kunal's desk and said, "Congratulations. You'll be good at it." I couldn't tell you what he felt. In the team meeting that afternoon, when Kunal presented the new plan, Tejas asked two sharp questions, and I tensed. But they were fair questions, and then he offered to take the hardest client. A week later he booked a meeting with our manager; I heard he asked, "What would I have needed to show?" He didn't sulk in the pantry the way some of us would have. I'm still not sure how he did it.

qa.q: Who got the team lead post?
qa.a: Kunal.

qa.q: What might Tejas have been feeling when he went very still and walked out?
qa.a: Tejas was probably hurt and envious, maybe angry, and stepped away to calm down before reacting.

qa.q: Which of Tejas's actions turned envy into something useful?
qa.a: Taking time out, congratulating Kunal, asking fair questions, volunteering for the hardest client, and asking the manager what he would need to show.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt when Tejas congratulated him?
qa.a: Kunal was probably relieved and grateful, perhaps a little awkward, knowing Tejas had wanted the role.

grounding: A colleague observes a young man handle the envy of being passed over for promotion professionally.

passage:
Monday. At the all-hands, the director praised Deepika's client pitch by name, twice. Asif, who had built half the slides, clapped and felt his jaw lock. At lunch he said to a colleague, "Nice to present other people's work." It came out uglier than he meant.
Thursday. Deepika stopped by his desk. "Someone told me what you said. I did mention your slides to the director. She just didn't repeat it." Asif's face burned. He mumbled something, and she left. That night he couldn't sleep. The truth was he wanted to be seen, and he had never once asked to present.
Two weeks later. Asif asked his manager if he could present the next pitch. He also apologised to Deepika properly, over coffee, without excuses. She said, "Want to co-present? I'll take questions, you take the numbers." The pitch went well. When the director praised them both, he noticed his jaw stayed loose.

qa.q: How many times did the director praise Deepika by name?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when he clapped with his jaw locked?
qa.a: Asif felt envious and resentful, wanting credit for the slides he had built.

qa.q: What did Asif do to repair the damage and address the real problem?
qa.a: He apologised properly without excuses and asked to present, facing his wish to be seen instead of sniping.

qa.q: How might Deepika have felt hearing about the lunch comment?
qa.a: Deepika was probably hurt and wanted to set the record straight, yet generous enough to offer co-presenting later.

grounding: Over two weeks, a young man moves from envious sniping at a colleague to an apology and asking to be seen.

subtype: Managing Anger, Envy & Ego at Work
passage: Farida, you're angry that the new girl got the conference slot. Let old Ramesh Uncle tell you about Joseph. When I was twenty-six at the railway coach workshop in Perambur, Joseph joined as a junior, sharp as a blade. Within a year the chief engineer asked Joseph, not me, to lead the new coach design. I was furious. I told everyone Joseph was a flatterer. I stopped sharing my calculations with him. For six months the project limped, because he needed load figures only I had. Then one night the chief called us both in and said, "Work together, or you're both off it." I went home ashamed; I knew I had been hurting the work to hurt him. Next morning I brought Joseph my notebooks. We finished eight weeks late, but that coach ran for thirty years, and we became friends. So feel the anger, Farida. Then ask whether it's feeding the work or eating it.

qa.q: Where did Ramesh work at twenty-six?
qa.a: At the railway coach workshop in Perambur.

qa.q: What was young Ramesh feeling when Joseph was chosen to lead?
qa.a: Ramesh felt furious and envious at being passed over for a junior.

qa.q: What was Ramesh's turning point, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Bringing Joseph the notebooks after the chief's warning; it put the work above his ego and let the project finish.

qa.q: How might Joseph have experienced those six months?
qa.a: Joseph was probably frustrated and isolated, blocked from figures he needed and hearing himself called a flatterer.

grounding: An older engineer tells a young woman how his envy of a rival nearly sank a project, and how he let it go.

passage:
Thursday night
Nearly a disaster today. I used the drafting assistant to write the research section of the brief for Rukmini Ma'am, the senior partner. It cited four judgments. They looked perfect. At 5 p.m. she asked me to pull the full text of the third one. I couldn't find it anywhere. Because it didn't exist. The tool had invented it.
She didn't shout. She asked, "Did you read them?" I said no. Worst feeling of my year.
We fixed it by nine: I found two real judgments that actually said what we needed. She said, "Use the tool to find leads. You're still the lawyer."
New rules for me: every citation, I open and read. And once a week I'll research one question fully by hand, so I don't forget how.
— Amandeep

qa.q: How many judgments did the assistant cite?
qa.a: Four judgments.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when Rukmini Ma'am asked 'Did you read them?'
qa.a: Amandeep felt deeply ashamed, calling it the worst feeling of the year.

qa.q: Which of Amandeep's new rules protect both accuracy and skill?
qa.a: Opening and reading every citation, and researching one question fully by hand each week so the skill isn't lost.

qa.q: How might Rukmini Ma'am see the incident?
qa.a: She treats it as a serious but teachable mistake, staying calm and making clear that accountability stays with the lawyer.

grounding: A young associate's diary shows an AI tool inventing a legal citation, and new rules for verification and keeping skills.

passage: The new phone app promised to identify crop disease from a single photo, and the agriculture department had asked Chetan, the young extension officer, to use it in the villages around Solapur. At Sonali's pomegranate orchard he photographed a spotted leaf. The app said "bacterial blight, 94 percent" and suggested a spray. Sonali, who had farmed these trees for nine years, frowned. "Blight spots look different. These came after the hailstorm." Chetan hesitated. It would be easy to trust the screen. But if the spray was wrong, Sonali would lose money and the soil would take the chemicals for nothing. He took three samples to the district lab instead. The result came back a week later: hail damage, no disease. Chetan wrote to the department suggesting that every app result be checked by an officer or lab before any spray was advised. Sonali sent him a box of pomegranates.

qa.q: How long had Sonali farmed the trees?
qa.a: Nine years.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when the app and Sonali disagreed?
qa.a: Chetan felt uncertain and tempted to trust the screen, but uneasy about the cost of being wrong.

qa.q: How did Chetan keep accountability while using the app?
qa.a: He treated its answer as a lead, sent samples to the district lab, and proposed that every app result be checked before a spray is advised.

qa.q: How might Sonali see the app after this?
qa.a: Sonali probably sees it as a tool that can be wrong, and feels respected that her experience was taken seriously.

grounding: A young extension officer in rural Maharashtra checks an AI crop app's answer instead of passing it on blindly.

passage: The video reached the village group chat in Buldhana district on a Sunday morning: a blurry clip of men dragging a child into a van, captioned "Kidnappers in our area. Beware of strangers." By noon two traders selling steel utensils had been surrounded near the bus stop. Tushar, who taught at the zilla parishad school, felt his stomach knot. He had seen the clip before. He searched using a still from the video and found it in a news report from another country, four years old, about a film shoot. He ran to the bus stop, where Sarpanch Ramesh was trying to calm the crowd, and showed him the old report. Ramesh read it slowly, called the police station, and told the crowd the video was fake. The traders were escorted out safely. That evening Tushar posted the original report in the group, with one line: "Please check before forwarding."

qa.q: What were the two traders selling?
qa.a: Steel utensils.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when the traders were surrounded?
qa.a: Tushar felt a knot of fear and urgency, knowing the clip could lead to real harm.

qa.q: How did Tushar verify the video and stop the harm?
qa.a: He traced the clip to an old foreign report about a film shoot, showed the sarpanch, who called the police and told the crowd, and posted the original in the group.

qa.q: How might the traders have felt when surrounded?
qa.a: The traders were probably terrified and confused, facing an angry crowd over something they had nothing to do with.

grounding: In a village, a young teacher verifies a viral kidnapping clip as fake and helps stop a crowd from harming strangers.

passage: Camila was three weeks into her job as a junior producer at a news website in Dublin when a photo exploded across social media: a well-known bridge over the Liffey, half underwater, cars floating. Fifty thousand shares in an hour. Her editor wanted it up. "Everyone else is running it." Liam, a senior producer, leaned over. "Check it first." Camila zoomed in. The water reflected sunlight, but the sky was grey. One car had four headlights on one side. She searched for the image and found no earlier copy and no photographer, and the flood-monitoring service showed normal river levels. She rang a council press officer, who said the bridge was dry. Camila told her editor it looked AI-generated. They ran a short piece instead: "Viral flood image is fake: here's how we checked." It became their most-read story of the week.

qa.q: How many shares did the photo get in an hour?
qa.a: Fifty thousand.

qa.q: What was Camila feeling under the editor's pressure to run it?
qa.a: Camila was probably nervous and pressured as a junior, but uneasy enough to check first.

qa.q: Which checks showed the photo was fake?
qa.a: Sunlit reflections under a grey sky, a car with four headlights on one side, no earlier copy or photographer, normal river levels, and a council officer confirming the bridge was dry.

qa.q: How might the editor see Camila's check after the story's success?
qa.a: The editor, who wanted to rush it, probably felt relieved and impressed that verifying became the week's most-read story.

grounding: A junior news producer in Ireland verifies a viral flood image as synthetic before sharing it.

passage: I'm Disha, Baljeet's flatmate. Last year she went through what I called her "phone diet". I don't know everything she was thinking; I saw what she did. One Sunday she sat at the dining table with her phone and a notebook, deleting apps one by one and writing down why she kept the rest: maps, banking, the family chat, a meditation timer. Fourteen apps went. Then she bought a cheap basic phone and carried only that on Saturdays. The first Saturday she kept patting her pocket. By the fourth she was reading novels on the balcony and calling her Nani instead of texting. She kept one news subscription she paid for and dropped the free feeds. She still used her laptop for work, of course. She just decided what came into her day. I copied half of it. I'm still not brave enough for the basic phone.

qa.q: How many apps did Baljeet delete?
qa.a: Fourteen apps.

qa.q: What might Baljeet have been feeling on the first Saturday with the basic phone?
qa.a: Baljeet seemed restless and uneasy, patting a pocket and missing the old habit.

qa.q: What made Baljeet's approach deliberate rather than simply cutting back?
qa.a: She wrote a reason for every app she kept, chose a paid news source over free feeds, and set a regular phone-light day.

qa.q: How does Disha see the change?
qa.a: Disha admires it enough to copy half of it, though not yet brave enough for the basic phone.

grounding: A flatmate describes a young woman choosing her apps and information sources deliberately.

passage:
March. Mehak's phone buzzed ninety times on an ordinary Tuesday: work chat, email, three shopping apps, a news app, the building group. She answered her manager Nandini's messages at 11 p.m. because the notification was there. She felt busy all the time and did nothing deep.
April. After forgetting a friend's birthday dinner, she spent a Saturday deciding what deserved her attention. Notifications off for everything except calls and family. Work chat only on the laptop, only between nine and seven. News once a day, in the evening. She told Nandini, nervously, "If something is urgent after seven, please call me." Nandini said, "Honestly, I'll do the same."
June. Mehak's phone buzzed eleven times on a Tuesday. She finished a report she had dodged for weeks in one long morning. Nandini called her after seven only once, for a real emergency, and Mehak didn't mind at all.

qa.q: How many times did Mehak's phone buzz on a Tuesday in June?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she asked Nandini to call if something was urgent?
qa.a: Mehak felt nervous about how Nandini would react to the new limits.

qa.q: Which choices made Mehak's technology use deliberate?
qa.a: Turning off notifications except calls and family, keeping work chat to laptop hours, and reading news once a day.

qa.q: How does Nandini respond to Mehak's limit?
qa.a: Nandini welcomes it and adopts it herself, calling after hours only for a real emergency.

grounding: Over three months, a young professional replaces default notifications with deliberate choices about attention.

passage: Sabina, you say you can't stop scrolling the news. Let your Hansa Khala tell you something from before phones. When I was twenty-five, working at a newspaper in Hyderabad, the new cable channels arrived with news all day and all night. I kept the TV on from waking to sleeping, afraid to miss anything. I felt informed and exhausted, and I started snapping at people. One evening my editor, a grey-haired man called Mr Qadri, said, "Hansa, you're reading everything and thinking nothing." That stung. So I made rules. TV news once, at nine. One good newspaper, read with a pen. Anything I repeated at work, I checked with a second source first. My head cleared. My writing got better. Now you carry a hundred cable channels in your pocket. Same choice, Sabina. Decide what comes in, or it decides for you.

qa.q: Where did Hansa work at twenty-five?
qa.a: At a newspaper in Hyderabad.

qa.q: What was young Hansa feeling when Mr Qadri said she was reading everything and thinking nothing?
qa.a: Hansa felt stung and hurt, but it made her rethink her habits.

qa.q: What rules did Hansa make, and why did they help?
qa.a: News on TV once at nine, one good newspaper read with a pen, and a second source before repeating anything; they turned endless intake into focused thinking.

qa.q: How might Mr Qadri have seen young Hansa?
qa.a: Mr Qadri probably saw a capable young journalist wearing herself out, and cared enough to say it bluntly.

grounding: An aunt tells a young woman how, at twenty-five, she chose her news diet deliberately instead of by default.

passage: When Rafiq and I married, both our families said the same thing: "Buy a flat. Rent is money thrown away." I, Bhavna, nearly believed them. We saw six flats in Pune in a month. Then I sat down with a spreadsheet and a fee-only financial adviser a colleague recommended. She didn't tell us what to do. She showed us the whole picture: the down payment would empty our savings, the EMI would be almost half our pay, and both our jobs might move cities within two years. For us, for now, renting meant flexibility. She also asked, "Do you have term life and health cover? Anything put aside for retirement?" We had neither. That was more urgent than a flat. We took proper cover and started a small monthly retirement contribution. My mother still sighs about the rent. Maybe in five years we'll buy. But we'll be choosing, not following.

qa.q: How many flats did they see in a month?
qa.a: Six flats.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when both families insisted on buying?
qa.a: Bhavna felt pressured and nearly convinced, unsure whether the family advice fitted their situation.

qa.q: Why did seeing a fee-only adviser help this decision?
qa.a: The adviser laid out the full picture without selling anything, which showed gaps in insurance and retirement savings that mattered more for them right now.

qa.q: How does Bhavna's mother see the decision to rent?
qa.a: Her mother still sighs about the rent, probably worried they are missing security, even if she accepts it.

grounding: A young married adult compares renting and buying with a qualified adviser and prioritises insurance and retirement basics.

passage: HR benefits officer's note, onboarding follow-up. Nilesh (joined in March) came in because a colleague, Rehana, told him he had opted out of the company's voluntary retirement contribution and the group health top-up without reading them. He admitted he had ticked "no" to anything that reduced his take-home pay; he sends money home and is paying off a two-wheeler loan. I didn't tell him what to choose. I explained what each option does, what the company adds, and that the health top-up covers his parents too. I suggested he speak to a registered adviser about his full picture and gave him the list the company provides. He chose to join the health top-up now and to revisit retirement in six months. He looked relieved to understand the forms. I have set a reminder for September. — Ms Joseph, HR benefits

qa.q: Who told Nilesh he had opted out?
qa.a: A colleague, Rehana.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have been feeling when he admitted ticking 'no' to everything?
qa.a: Nilesh was probably embarrassed and a little anxious, worried about the money he sends home and his loan.

qa.q: What made Ms Joseph's approach appropriate?
qa.a: She explained the options without choosing for him, pointed him to a registered adviser, and set a reminder to revisit.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel about having told Nilesh?
qa.a: Rehana probably felt glad to have spoken up, especially since Nilesh then joined the health top-up that covers his parents.

grounding: An HR note shows a young employee learning what his insurance and retirement options mean and seeking qualified advice.

passage:
Wednesday
Papa's surgery bill came today. Four lakh. He never had health insurance; he always said, "God will provide." God, it turns out, provided Papa's old fixed deposits, all of them. He's recovering, thank God. But he's fifty-eight and has nothing left for retirement.
Damini sat with me on the hospital bench tonight while I did the maths I've avoided since I started working. No health cover of my own beyond the office one. Nothing for retirement except the office deduction I've never looked at.
We made a list, not a plan: proper health cover for both of us and for Mummy-Papa, find out what the office deduction actually is, and book a registered financial adviser, not the insurance agent from Papa's building who keeps calling.
Everyone says I have time. Tonight it feels like the best time is now.
— Sachin

qa.q: How much was Papa's surgery bill?
qa.a: Four lakh.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling on the hospital bench?
qa.a: Sachin felt shaken and anxious, seeing how exposed Sachin's own finances were after Papa's savings were wiped out.

qa.q: Why is booking a registered adviser rather than the building's insurance agent a sensible step?
qa.a: A registered adviser can look at Sachin's whole situation without pushing a particular product.

qa.q: How might Papa feel about his savings being gone?
qa.a: Papa is probably relieved to be recovering but worried, perhaps regretful, about having nothing left for retirement.

grounding: After an uninsured father's surgery, a young adult's diary lists first steps on insurance and retirement with qualified help.

passage: When I, Trisha, got my first big raise last year, I didn't notice my spending grow. It just did. A flat with a balcony because "I deserved it". A new phone because my old one looked embarrassing in meetings. Weekend brunches at the café where everyone from work went. Six months later my salary was forty percent higher and my savings were exactly where they had been. My friend Parul, who earns less than me, had quietly saved for a trip to Ladakh. I asked how. She said, "I only upgrade when something is broken or making me miserable. Not when someone at work has a nicer one." That stayed with me. I went through my spending and marked each item: need, want, or image. The image column was long. I kept the balcony flat, because I truly love it. I stopped the brunches I only went to so I'd be seen.

qa.q: How much higher was Trisha's salary after six months?
qa.a: Forty percent higher.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling on comparing savings with Parul?
qa.a: Trisha felt surprised and a little embarrassed that a friend earning less had saved more.

qa.q: How did sorting spending into need, want and image help?
qa.a: It separated real value, like the balcony, from spending for appearances, like brunches to be seen, so Trisha could cut the right things.

qa.q: How might Parul feel about Trisha asking?
qa.a: Parul probably felt pleased to share, and quietly glad her simple habit helped a friend.

grounding: A young professional looks back on lifestyle creep after a raise and learns to separate needs from image.

passage: Employee wellbeing counsellor's note. Jasleen (sales) came in saying she felt "always broke" despite two raises in eighteen months. She wasn't in crisis, just stressed. We looked at her month together, without judgement. Rent had doubled after she moved closer to her team's favourite neighbourhood; three subscriptions she had forgotten; a car loan taken soon after her colleague Vidya bought a car. She said, "I didn't even want the car. I just didn't want to be the only one on the metro." That was the real moment. She decided, not me, to keep the flat, cancel the subscriptions, and think about selling the car. She also asked for the company's list of registered financial advisers. I suggested she talk to Vidya honestly; she laughed and said Vidya had admitted the same thing. We meet again in a month.

qa.q: How many raises had Jasleen had in eighteen months?
qa.a: Two raises.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling when she said she didn't even want the car?
qa.a: Jasleen felt a mix of relief and embarrassment, admitting she bought it to avoid feeling left out.

qa.q: What made the counsellor's approach helpful?
qa.a: Looking at the month without judgement, letting Jasleen make the decisions, and pointing her to registered advisers.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel about Jasleen's honesty?
qa.a: Vidya seems to have felt the same pressure, so hearing Jasleen admit it may bring relief and shared understanding.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young employee realising her rising costs came from status spending, not needs.

passage:
Saturday
Mohit's wedding plans arrived in the group chat today: a bachelor trip to Goa, matching sherwanis for all six of us, and a cocktail night at a hotel. My share would be more than two months' rent. Everyone replied with fire emojis. I stared at my phone for an hour.
I love Mohit. I've known him since Class 3. But I've just finished paying off my laptop, and I'm saving to move out of my uncle's house.
So I called him instead of typing. I said, "Bro, I'm coming to everything that matters. I can't do Goa or the matching sherwani. I'll wear my best suit and be there from haldi to vidaai." He went quiet, then said, "Honestly, half the group can't afford Goa either. They're too scared to say."
Maybe I'll suggest a day trip to Lonavala instead. I felt lighter after that call than after my last raise.
— Francis

qa.q: How many friends were to wear matching sherwanis?
qa.a: All six.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling while staring at the phone for an hour?
qa.a: Francis felt torn and stressed, loving Mohit but worried about the cost.

qa.q: What made Francis's call a good way to handle the pressure?
qa.a: Francis spoke directly, said what was possible, committed to what mattered, and the honesty revealed that others felt the same.

qa.q: How does Mohit react to Francis's call?
qa.a: Mohit goes quiet, then admits half the group can't afford it either, suggesting relief that someone finally said it.

grounding: A diary shows a young adult declining costly wedding extras while staying close to a friend.

passage: Irfan, you say the ward meeting is a waste of time. Let your Urmila Aunty tell you about the first one I went to, at twenty-four, in Bhopal. Our lane flooded every monsoon. I went in angry, ready to shout at the corporator. An old engineer at the back stopped me. He showed me the budget sheet on the notice board: that year the ward had money for either a new drain or a park, not both. The park had been promised to the colony next door, where children had nowhere to play. Suddenly it wasn't villains and victims. It was a trade-off. So I didn't shout. I collected photos of the flooding from twenty households, presented them at the next meeting, and asked whether the drain could come first with the park in next year's plan. The colony agreed, for a written promise. It took eighteen months, but the lane hasn't flooded since. Come with me on Sunday, Irfan.

qa.q: What choice did the ward budget force that year?
qa.a: Either a new drain or a park, not both.

qa.q: What was young Urmila feeling when she went to the first meeting?
qa.a: Urmila felt angry, ready to shout at the corporator about the flooding.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it work?
qa.a: Seeing the budget trade-off, she gathered photos from twenty households and proposed an order with a written promise, which the other colony could accept.

qa.q: How might the colony next door have seen Urmila's proposal?
qa.a: They probably worried about losing the promised park, but the written promise for the next year made it fair enough to agree.

grounding: An aunt tells a young man how, at twenty-four, she learned to see a local budget trade-off and take part constructively.

passage: The city's draft plan to cut three bus routes in Kolkata was open for public comment for only two more days, and the form was online, in English, on a website that crashed twice. Bidisha, a schoolteacher in Behala, read the plan on her lunch break. One of the cut routes was the bus her neighbour, Sudha Mashi, took to the hospital every week. Bidisha understood the reason: the routes were losing money, and the new metro line covered part of the area. But the metro station was two kilometres from Sudha Mashi's lane. That evening she knocked on doors with a printed copy, explained the plan in Bengali, and wrote down what twelve neighbours said. Then she typed a clear comment: the saving made sense, but the lane needed a feeder bus to the metro. She submitted it at 11:40 p.m., with Sudha Mashi's name on it too. Three months later a small feeder bus started.

qa.q: How far was the metro station from Sudha Mashi's lane?
qa.a: Two kilometres.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling about the plan to cut the route?
qa.a: Bidisha felt concerned for Sudha Mashi, even though she understood why the routes were losing money.

qa.q: How did Bidisha take part constructively under the tight deadline?
qa.a: She understood the trade-off, gathered neighbours' views in Bengali, and submitted a specific solution, a feeder bus, before the deadline.

qa.q: How might Sudha Mashi have felt seeing the feeder bus start?
qa.a: Sudha Mashi probably felt relieved and valued, her hospital trips protected and her voice included.

grounding: With little time and an awkward online form, a young teacher weighs a transport policy's trade-offs and submits a constructive comment.

passage: When the Chandigarh municipal corporation announced paid parking in the Sector 22 market, Simran was furious. "They just want our money," she said. Sudha, her colleague, who studied planning in the evenings, wasn't sure. On the bus home she read the policy document: the free parking was full by 9 a.m., shoppers circled for twenty minutes, and the fees would fund a shuttle from the bus stand. She also found what worried her: nothing for the street vendors who parked their carts there. On Saturday she went to the ward committee's open meeting, a folding-chair room above a sweet shop. She didn't argue against the whole policy. She asked one question: "Where do the vendors go?" The officer admitted it hadn't been planned. The committee agreed to mark a vendor zone before fees started. Simran, who had come along reluctantly, said afterwards, "I thought these meetings were for shouting."

qa.q: What would the parking fees fund?
qa.a: A shuttle from the bus stand.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling after reading the policy document?
qa.a: Sudha felt uncertain and curious, seeing real benefits but worried about the vendors.

qa.q: Why was Sudha's single question effective?
qa.a: It accepted the policy's aim but pointed to a gap, the vendors, which officials could act on.

qa.q: How does Simran's view of the meeting change?
qa.a: Simran came reluctantly, expecting shouting, and was surprised to see one calm question lead to a change.

grounding: A young woman in Chandigarh reads a parking policy's trade-offs and takes part constructively in a ward meeting.
